hardwareProjects.title: Smart Temperature Monitor with Auto Alert
hardwareProjects.description:
Time: 3–4 hours    Difficulty: Beginner⏱ 🎯  
This is your very first IoT project. A DHT22 sensor connected to Raspberry Pi reads temperature and humidity 
every 10 seconds. If temperature goes above your set limit, it sends you an email automatically. This teaches 
you the complete sensor-to-alert pipeline.
hardware: DHT22 or DHT11 temperature and humidity sensor
10 kΩ resistor (for DHT signal pin — optional but recommended)
hardwareProjects.wiring:
DHT22 VCC → Pi Pin 1 (3.3V)
DHT22 GND → Pi Pin 6 (GND)
DHT22 DATA → Pi Pin 7 (GPIO4)
Optional: 10kΩ resistor between VCC and DATA pin
steps: Step 1: Install library — Open terminal on Pi: sudo pip3 install adafruit-circuitpython-dht
Step 2: Wire the sensor — Connect DHT22 VCC → Pi 3.3V (Pin 1), GND → Pi GND (Pin 6), DATA → Pi
Step 3: Create .env file — Create /home/pi/project1/.env and add your email credentials
Step 4: Write the code — Create /home/pi/project1/monitor.py with the code below
Step 5: Test manually — Run: python3 monitor.py — you should see readings every 10 seconds
Step 6: Set temperature limit — Change ALERT_TEMP in the code to your desired threshold
Step 7: Make it run forever — Use nohup or create a systemd service
hardwareProjects.code:
# monitor.py — Smart Temperature Monitor
import time, smtplib, logging
import adafruit_dht
import board
from email.mime.text import MIMEText
from dotenv import load_dotenv
import os
load_dotenv()
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s %(message)s")
# ── SETTINGS ── (change these to your values)
ALERT_TEMP    = 35.0          # alert if temperature exceeds this
CHECK_INTERVAL = 10           # seconds between readings
EMAIL_FROM    = os.getenv("EMAIL_FROM")
EMAIL_TO      = os.getenv("EMAIL_TO")
EMAIL_PASS    = os.getenv("EMAIL_PASS")
# ── SENSOR SETUP ──
dht = adafruit_dht.DHT22(board.D4)   # GPIO pin 4
def send_alert(temp: float, humidity: float) -> None:
    """Send email alert when temperature is too high."""
    msg = MIMEText(f"ALERT!\nTemperature: {temp}°C\nHumidity: {humidity}%")
    msg["Subject"] = f"[HIGH TEMP] {temp}°C detected!"
    msg["From"]    = EMAIL_FROM
    msg["To"]      = EMAIL_TO
    with smtplib.SMTP_SSL("smtp.gmail.com", 465) as s:
        s.login(EMAIL_FROM, EMAIL_PASS)
        s.sendmail(EMAIL_FROM, EMAIL_TO, msg.as_string())
    logging.info("Alert email sent!")
last_alert_time = 0   # prevent spam: only alert once every 30 minutes
while True:
    try:
        temp     = dht.temperature
        humidity = dht.humidity
        logging.info(f"Temp={temp}°C  Humidity={humidity}%")

        # Check if alert needed and cooldown passed
        if temp > ALERT_TEMP and (time.time() - last_alert_time) > 1800:
            send_alert(temp, humidity)
            last_alert_time = time.time()
    except RuntimeError as e:
        # DHT sensors fail occasionally — just try again
        logging.warning(f"Sensor error (will retry): {e}")
    time.sleep(CHECK_INTERVAL)
whatYouLearn: How to read a real physical sensor using Python
How to send emails programmatically
Error handling for real hardware (sensors fail sometimes)
How to prevent spam alerts using cooldown logic
Logging — never use print() in production code
videoReferences: Python Email Sending Tutorial (Corey Schafer): youtube.com/watch?v=JRCJ6RtE3xU

hardwareProjects.title: MQTT Sensor Dashboard — Real-Time Web Display
hardwareProjects.description:
Time: 5–6 hours    Difficulty: Beginner-Intermediate⏱ 🎯  
This project builds a real-time web dashboard that shows live sensor data. Your Raspberry Pi publishes sensor 
readings via MQTT. A Flask web application subscribes to MQTT and displays the data in a nice chart that  
updates every second. This is the foundation for all industrial IoT dashboards.
hardware: Laptop or second computer for viewing dashboard
steps: Step 1: Install Mosquitto broker — sudo apt install -y mosquitto mosquitto-clients && sudo systemctl
Step 2: Test MQTT manually — Open two terminals. In terminal 1: mosquitto_sub -t test/#. In terminal
Step 3: Install Python libraries — pip3 install paho-mqtt flask flask-socketio
Step 4: Create publisher — publisher.py reads DHT22 and publishes to MQTT topic sensors/pi001/dht22
Step 5: Create dashboard app — dashboard.py is a Flask app that subscribes to MQTT and pushes
Step 6: Create HTML template — templates/index.html is the web page with Chart.js graphs
Step 7: Run both scripts — Terminal 1: python3 publisher.py. Terminal 2: python3 dashboard.py. Open
hardwareProjects.code:
# publisher.py — reads sensor and publishes to MQTT

import paho.mqtt.client as mqtt
import adafruit_dht, board, time, json, logging
from datetime import datetime
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
DEVICE_ID = "pi001"
MQTT_HOST  = "localhost"
# Setup MQTT client
client = mqtt.Client(client_id=f"publisher_{DEVICE_ID}")
client.connect(MQTT_HOST, 1883, keepalive=60)
client.loop_start()   # background thread handles connection
# Setup sensor
dht = adafruit_dht.DHT22(board.D4)
while True:
    try:
        payload = json.dumps({
            "device_id": DEVICE_ID,
            "temperature": dht.temperature,
            "humidity": dht.humidity,
            "timestamp": datetime.utcnow().isoformat()
        })
        topic = f"sensors/{DEVICE_ID}/dht22"
        client.publish(topic, payload, qos=1)
        logging.info(f"Published: {payload[:60]}...")
    except RuntimeError as e:
        logging.warning(f"Sensor error: {e}")
    time.sleep(5)
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# dashboard.py — Flask app with real-time MQTT updates
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from flask import Flask, render_template
from flask_socketio import SocketIO, emit
import paho.mqtt.client as mqtt
import json, threading
app = Flask(__name__)
socketio = SocketIO(app, cors_allowed_origins="*")
# MQTT message handler — runs in background thread
def on_message(client, userdata, msg):
    data = json.loads(msg.payload.decode())
    # Send data to all connected browsers

    socketio.emit("sensor_update", data)
# Setup MQTT subscriber
mqtt_client = mqtt.Client("dashboard")
mqtt_client.on_message = on_message
mqtt_client.connect("localhost", 1883)
mqtt_client.subscribe("sensors/#", qos=1)
# Start MQTT in background thread
mqtt_thread = threading.Thread(target=mqtt_client.loop_forever, daemon=True)
mqtt_thread.start()
@app.route("/")
def index(): return render_template("index.html")
if __name__ == "__main__":
    socketio.run(app, host="0.0.0.0", port=5000)
whatYouLearn: MQTT publish-subscribe pattern — the foundation of all IoT communication
How Flask handles web requests
Real-time browser updates using WebSocket (SocketIO)
Threading — running MQTT and web server at the same time
JSON — the universal IoT data format

hardwareProjects.title: Edge AI Image Classifier — Run AI on Raspberry Pi
hardwareProjects.description:
Time: 6–8 hours    Difficulty: Intermediate⏱ 🎯  
This is the most important project for your Edge AI career. You run a TensorFlow Lite image classification model 
directly on the Raspberry Pi — no internet required. Point the camera at any object and the Pi tells you what it 
is within 30ms. This demonstrates the core concept of Edge AI.
hardware: Raspberry Pi Camera Module 3 (or Camera Module 2)
Heatsink case for Pi (prevents thermal throttling during inference)
hardwareProjects.wiring:
Pi Camera Module → CSI ribbon cable → Pi Camera port (small slot near HDMI)
No GPIO wiring needed for camera module
steps: Step 1: Enable camera — sudo raspi-config → Interface Options → Camera → Enable → Reboot
Step 2: Install libraries — pip3 install tflite-runtime picamera2 numpy Pillow
Step 3: Download model — Download MobileNet V3 TFLite model from TensorFlow Hub — link in code
Step 4: Download labels — Download ImageNet labels file (1000 classes) — link in code comments
Step 5: Run single image test — Test with a photo file first before using live camera
Step 6: Run live classification — Run with --live flag to classify camera feed in real time
Step 7: Measure speed — The code automatically measures and prints inference time per frame
hardwareProjects.code:
# edge_classifier.py — Edge AI Image Classifier on Raspberry Pi
# Model download: 
tfhub.dev/tensorflow/lite-model/mobilenet_v3_large_100_224/classification

# Labels download: 
storage.googleapis.com/download.tensorflow.org/data/ImageNetLabels.txt
import tflite_runtime.interpreter as tflite
import numpy as np
from PIL import Image
import time, argparse, logging
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
# ── Model Loading ──
def load_model(model_path: str) -> tflite.Interpreter:
    """Load TFLite model and allocate memory."""
    interp = tflite.Interpreter(model_path=model_path)
    interp.allocate_tensors()
    logging.info(f"Model loaded: {model_path}")
    return interp
def load_labels(labels_path: str) -> list[str]:
    """Load class label names."""
    with open(labels_path, "r") as f:
        return [line.strip() for line in f.readlines()]
# ── Image Preprocessing ──
def preprocess(image_path: str, size: int = 224) -> np.ndarray:
    """Resize and normalise image for MobileNet input."""
    img = Image.open(image_path).convert("RGB")
    img = img.resize((size, size))        # resize to 224x224
    arr = np.array(img, dtype=np.float32) # convert to numpy
    arr = arr / 255.0                     # normalise to [0, 1]
    arr = np.expand_dims(arr, axis=0)     # add batch dimension: (1, 224, 224, 3)
    return arr
# ── Inference ──
def classify(interp: tflite.Interpreter,
             image: np.ndarray,
             labels: list[str],
             top_k: int = 3) -> list[tuple[str, float]]:
    """Run inference and return top K predictions."""
    input_idx  = interp.get_input_details()[0]["index"]
    output_idx = interp.get_output_details()[0]["index"]
    interp.set_tensor(input_idx, image)
    t_start = time.perf_counter()
    interp.invoke()

    latency_ms = (time.perf_counter() - t_start) * 1000
    scores = interp.get_tensor(output_idx)[0]  # shape: (1000,)
    top_indices = np.argsort(scores)[::-1][:top_k]
    results = [(labels[i], float(scores[i])) for i in top_indices]
    logging.info(f"Inference: {latency_ms:.1f}ms")
    return results
# ── Main ──
if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--model",  default="mobilenet_v3.tflite")
    parser.add_argument("--labels", default="labels.txt")
    parser.add_argument("--image",  default=None)
    parser.add_argument("--live",   action="store_true")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    interp = load_model(args.model)
    labels = load_labels(args.labels)
    if args.image:
        # Classify a single image file
        img = preprocess(args.image)
        results = classify(interp, img, labels)
        print("\nTop 3 Predictions:")
        for name, score in results:
            print(f"  {name:30s} {score*100:.1f}%")
    elif args.live:
        # Live camera classification
        from picamera2 import Picamera2
        cam = Picamera2()
        cam.configure(cam.create_preview_configuration(
            main={"size": (640, 480), "format": "RGB888"}
        ))
        cam.start()
        print("\nLive classification started. Press Ctrl+C to stop.")
        while True:
            frame = cam.capture_array()          # get camera frame
            pil_img = Image.fromarray(frame)
            pil_img = pil_img.resize((224, 224))
            arr = np.array(pil_img, dtype=np.float32) / 255.0
            arr = np.expand_dims(arr, 0)
            results = classify(interp, arr, labels)
            top_label, top_score = results[0]

            print(f"\r{top_label:30s} {top_score*100:.0f}%", end="", flush=True)
whatYouLearn: TensorFlow Lite runtime — how to load and run a model
Image preprocessing — why normalisation to [0,1] matters
Inference pipeline: load model → preprocess image → invoke → read output
Latency measurement — how to benchmark your edge AI system
argparse — professional command-line interface for Python scripts

hardwareProjects.title: AI-Powered Anomaly Detector with Claude Analysis
hardwareProjects.description:
Time: 6–8 hours    Difficulty: Intermediate⏱ 🎯  
This project combines your sensor pipeline (Project 2) with the Claude API (Section 1) to create an intelligent  
monitoring system. When the Pi detects an unusual sensor reading, it does not just send an alert — it asks  
Claude to explain what might be wrong and what to do. This is the AI-augmented IoT system that impresses  
recruiters.
hardwareProjects.wiring:
DHT22 → Pi GPIO4 (same as Project 1)
Mosquitto MQTT broker running on Pi
steps: Step 1: Get Claude API key — console.anthropic.com → Create API key → add to .env file as
Step 2: Install Claude library — pip3 install anthropic
Step 3: Create the analyser — Create analyser.py — this subscribes to MQTT and calls Claude when
Step 4: Set your thresholds — Edit NORMAL_TEMP_RANGE and NORMAL_HUMIDITY_RANGE in the
Step 5: Run the system — Terminal 1: python3 publisher.py (from Project 2). Terminal 2: python3
Step 6: Trigger an anomaly — Put your hand around DHT22 sensor to raise temperature — watch the AI
hardwareProjects.code:
# analyser.py — AI-Powered Anomaly Detector with Claude
import paho.mqtt.client as mqtt
import anthropic, json, logging, os
from dotenv import load_dotenv
from datetime import datetime
from collections import deque
load_dotenv()
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s %(message)s")
# ── SETTINGS ──
NORMAL_TEMP_RANGE     = (15.0, 35.0)   # (min, max) degrees Celsius
NORMAL_HUMIDITY_RANGE = (30.0, 80.0)   # (min, max) percent
HISTORY_SIZE          = 10              # remember last 10 readings for context
# ── CLAUDE SETUP ──
claude = anthropic.Anthropic()
SYSTEM_PROMPT = """
You are an expert IoT system diagnostic engineer.
When given sensor readings, you:
1. Identify what is abnormal and why
2. List 2 possible physical causes (simple language)
3. Give 1 immediate action to take
4. Rate urgency: LOW / MEDIUM / HIGH / CRITICAL
Keep response under 5 sentences. Be direct.
"""
def ask_claude(current: dict, history: list) -> str:
    """Ask Claude to analyse an anomalous reading."""
    history_text = "\n".join([
        f"  {r['timestamp']}: {r['temperature']}°C, {r['humidity']}%"
        for r in list(history)[-5:]  # last 5 readings for context
    ])
    user_message = f"""
Current reading (ANOMALOUS):
  Temperature: {current['temperature']}°C (Normal: 15-35°C)
  Humidity: {current['humidity']}% (Normal: 30-80%)
  Time: {current['timestamp']}
Recent history (last 5 readings):
{history_text}

What is happening and what should I do?
    """
    response = claude.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
        max_tokens=300,
        system=SYSTEM_PROMPT,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": user_message}]
    )
    return response.content[0].text
# ── ANOMALY DETECTION ──
def is_anomaly(data: dict) -> bool:
    """Check if reading is outside normal range."""
    temp_lo, temp_hi = NORMAL_TEMP_RANGE
    hum_lo, hum_hi   = NORMAL_HUMIDITY_RANGE
    return (data["temperature"] < temp_lo or data["temperature"] > temp_hi or
            data["humidity"] < hum_lo or data["humidity"] > hum_hi)
# ── MQTT SETUP ──
history = deque(maxlen=HISTORY_SIZE)
def on_message(client, userdata, msg):
    data = json.loads(msg.payload.decode())
    history.append(data)
    if is_anomaly(data):
        logging.warning(f"ANOMALY DETECTED: {data}")
        print("\n" + "="*50)
        print("ANOMALY DETECTED!")
        print(f"Temperature: {data['temperature']}°C")
        print(f"Humidity:    {data['humidity']}%")
        print("\nAsking Claude AI for analysis...")
        analysis = ask_claude(data, history)
        print(f"\n  Claude Analysis:\n{analysis}")🤖
        print("="*50 + "\n")
    else:
        logging.info(f"Normal: {data['temperature']}°C, {data['humidity']}%")
client = mqtt.Client("ai_analyser")
client.on_message = on_message
client.connect("localhost", 1883)
client.subscribe("sensors/#", qos=1)
logging.info("AI Anomaly Analyser running. Waiting for sensor data...")
client.loop_forever()
whatYouLearn: How to integrate an AI API (Claude) into an IoT system
Contextual analysis — giving AI history improves its reasoning
Deque — efficient fixed-size history buffer in Python
Building a complete sensor-to-AI pipeline from scratch
Cost management — how to avoid spending too much on API calls (use cooldowns)

hardwareProjects.title: LangChain Conversational IoT Assistant
hardwareProjects.description:
Time: 8–10 hours    Difficulty: Intermediate-Advanced⏱ 🎯  
This project builds a chatbot that you can have a real conversation with about your IoT system. Unlike Project 4 
which gives one-off analyses, this assistant REMEMBERS previous messages. You can ask "What was the  
temperature an hour ago?" and then "Is that normal for this time of day?" and it connects the context.
hardware: Raspberry Pi 4 (or just your laptop for this project)

Step 2: Create database — Run the database setup section of the code to create sensor_history.db
Step 3: Populate with fake data — Run the data generator to create 24 hours of simulated sensor data
Step 4: Create the agent — Create iot_assistant.py with the code below

Step 6: Try complex queries — Ask "What was the average temperature yesterday?" or "Show me all
hardwareProjects.code:
# iot_assistant.py — LangChain Conversational IoT Assistant
import sqlite3, json, logging
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
from dotenv import load_dotenv

from langchain_anthropic import ChatAnthropic
from langchain.tools import tool
from langchain.agents import create_tool_calling_agent, AgentExecutor
from langchain.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate, MessagesPlaceholder
from langchain.memory import ConversationBufferWindowMemory
load_dotenv()
DB_PATH = "sensor_history.db"
# ── DATABASE TOOLS (what the agent can query) ──
@tool
def get_readings(sensor_type: str = "temperature", hours_ago: int = 1) -> str:
    """Get sensor readings from the last N hours. sensor_type: temperature or 
humidity."""
    since = datetime.utcnow() - timedelta(hours=hours_ago)
    with sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH) as conn:
        rows = conn.execute("""
            SELECT value, timestamp FROM readings
            WHERE sensor_type = ? AND timestamp > ?
            ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 50
        """, (sensor_type, since.isoformat())).fetchall()
    if not rows:
        return f"No {sensor_type} readings found in last {hours_ago} hour(s)"
    values = [r[0] for r in rows]
    return json.dumps({"count": len(rows), "min": min(values),
                      "max": max(values), "avg": round(sum(values)/len(values), 2),
                      "latest": values[0], "unit": "C" if sensor_type=="temperature" 
else "%"})
@tool
def count_anomalies(threshold: float = 35.0, days_ago: int = 1) -> str:
    """Count how many times temperature exceeded a threshold in last N days."""
    since = datetime.utcnow() - timedelta(days=days_ago)
    with sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH) as conn:
        count = conn.execute("""
            SELECT COUNT(*) FROM readings
            WHERE sensor_type="temperature" AND value > ? AND timestamp > ?
        """, (threshold, since.isoformat())).fetchone()[0]
    return f"Temperature exceeded {threshold}°C exactly {count} time(s) in last 
{days_ago} day(s)"
@tool
def get_current_reading() -> str:
    """Get the most recent sensor reading."""
    with sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH) as conn:
        row = conn.execute("""

            SELECT sensor_type, value, timestamp FROM readings
            ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 1
        """).fetchone()
    if row: return f"Latest: {row[0]}={row[1]} at {row[2]}"
    return "No readings found in database"
# ── LANGCHAIN AGENT WITH MEMORY ──
llm    = ChatAnthropic(model="claude-sonnet-4-6", temperature=0)
tools  = [get_readings, count_anomalies, get_current_reading]
prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([
    ("system", """You are a friendly IoT monitoring assistant.
    You help users understand their sensor data.
    Always use the available tools to get actual data before answering.
    Explain results in simple, non-technical language unless asked otherwise."""),
    MessagesPlaceholder(variable_name="chat_history"),  # conversation memory
    ("human", "{input}"),
    MessagesPlaceholder(variable_name="agent_scratchpad"),
])
memory = ConversationBufferWindowMemory(
    memory_key="chat_history",
    return_messages=True,
    k=10   # remember last 10 exchanges
)
agent    = create_tool_calling_agent(llm, tools, prompt)
executor = AgentExecutor(agent=agent, tools=tools,
                        memory=memory, verbose=False)
print("\n  IoT Assistant ready! (type 'exit' to quit)")🤖
print("Try: 'What is the current temperature?'")
print("Try: 'How many times did it overheat today?'\n")
while True:
    user_input = input("You: ").strip()
    if user_input.lower() in ["exit", "quit", "bye"]: break
    if not user_input: continue
    result = executor.invoke({"input": user_input})
    print(f"\nAssistant: {result['output']}\n")
whatYouLearn: LangChain agent framework — how tools + LLM + memory work together
Conversation memory — keeping context across messages
Database queries from within AI tools
How to design tools that an AI agent can use effectively
The difference between stateless AI (no memory) and stateful AI (with memory)

# predictor.py — Real-Time Vibration Fault Classifier
import tflite_runtime.interpreter as tflite
import numpy as np
import adafruit_adxl34x, board, busio
import time, logging, paho.mqtt.client as mqtt, json
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
CLASSES = ["normal", "imbalance_fault", "bearing_fault"]
SAMPLE_RATE = 100  # readings per second
WINDOW_SIZE = 50   # use 50 readings per classification
# ── Sensor Setup ──
i2c   = busio.I2C(board.SCL, board.SDA)
adxl  = adafruit_adxl34x.ADXL345(i2c)
adxl.range = adafruit_adxl34x.Range.RANGE_2_G
# ── Model Setup ──
interp = tflite.Interpreter("vibration_model.tflite")
interp.allocate_tensors()
in_idx  = interp.get_input_details()[0]["index"]
out_idx = interp.get_output_details()[0]["index"]
# ── Feature Extraction ──
def extract_features(window: list) -> np.ndarray:
    """Convert raw XYZ readings to statistical features."""
    arr = np.array(window)         # shape: (50, 3)
    x, y, z = arr[:,0], arr[:,1], arr[:,2]
    magnitude = np.sqrt(x**2 + y**2 + z**2)
    features = [
        magnitude.mean(), magnitude.std(),
        magnitude.max(), magnitude.min(),
        np.percentile(magnitude, 25),
        np.percentile(magnitude, 75),
        np.sqrt(np.mean(magnitude**2)),  # RMS (root mean square)
        float(np.fft.fft(magnitude)[:3].real.mean()),  # dominant frequency
    ]
    return np.array([features], dtype=np.float32)  # shape: (1, 8)
# ── MQTT Setup ──
mq = mqtt.Client("predictor")
mq.connect("localhost", 1883)
mq.loop_start()
# ── Main Loop ──

window = []
while True:
    x, y, z = adxl.acceleration
    window.append((x, y, z))
    if len(window) >= WINDOW_SIZE:
        features = extract_features(window)
        interp.set_tensor(in_idx, features)
        interp.invoke()
        probs   = interp.get_tensor(out_idx)[0]
        pred_id = np.argmax(probs)
        pred    = CLASSES[pred_id]
        conf    = probs[pred_id]
        result = {"prediction": pred, "confidence": float(conf), "time": 
time.time()}
        logging.info(f"Prediction: {pred} ({conf*100:.1f}%)")
        mq.publish("predictions/vibration", json.dumps(result))
        if pred != "normal":
            logging.warning(f"FAULT DETECTED: {pred}!")
            mq.publish("alerts/vibration", json.dumps(result), qos=1)
        window = []  # reset window
    time.sleep(1/SAMPLE_RATE)
whatYouLearn: Vibration analysis using FFT (Fast Fourier Transform) — used in industrial maintenance worldwide

from dotenv import load_dotenv

# Twilio credentials from .env

def send_whatsapp(to: str, message: str) -> None:

        body=message,
        from_=TWILIO_WHATSAPP,
        to=f"whatsapp:{to}"

@app.route("/webhook", methods=["POST"])
def webhook():
    """Handle incoming WhatsApp messages."""
    incoming = request.form.get("Body", "").lower().strip()
    sender   = request.form.get("From", "").replace("whatsapp:", "")
    resp = MessagingResponse()
    if "temperature" in incoming or "temp" in incoming:
        try:

            hum  = dht.humidity
            msg  = f"  Temperature: {temp}°C\n  Humidity: {hum}%"🌡️ 💧
        except RuntimeError:
            msg = "  Sensor error — please try again"❌
        resp.message(msg)
    elif "photo" in incoming or "camera" in incoming:
        cam = Picamera2()

        cam.capture_file("/tmp/snapshot.jpg")

        cam.stop()
        # Send image via Twilio media URL (requires hosted file)

capture image\n• status — check Pi status")

# backend/main.py — FastAPI + MongoDB + MQTT Backend
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware
from motor.motor_asyncio import AsyncIOMotorClient
import paho.mqtt.client as mqtt
import json, os, asyncio, threading
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
from dotenv import load_dotenv
load_dotenv()
app = FastAPI(title="AIoT Dashboard API")
# Allow React frontend to call this API
app.add_middleware(CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=["*"], allow_methods=["*"], allow_headers=["*"])
# ── MongoDB Setup ──
mongo = AsyncIOMotorClient(os.getenv("MONGO_URI"))
db    = mongo["aiot_database"]
# ── API Endpoints ──
@app.get("/readings/latest")
async def get_latest():
    """Get the 20 most recent sensor readings."""
    cursor = db.readings.find({}, {"_id": 0}).sort("timestamp", -1).limit(20)
    return await cursor.to_list(length=20)
@app.get("/readings/stats")
async def get_stats():
    """Get 24-hour statistics for all sensors."""
    since = datetime.utcnow() - timedelta(hours=24)
    pipeline = [
        {"$match": {"timestamp": {"$gt": since.isoformat()}}},
        {"$group": {"_id": "$sensor_type",
                    "avg": {"$avg": "$value"},
                    "max": {"$max": "$value"},
                    "min": {"$min": "$value"},
                    "count": {"$sum": 1}}}
    ]
    return await db.readings.aggregate(pipeline).to_list(length=10)
@app.get("/alerts")
async def get_alerts():
    """Get recent alerts."""

    cursor = db.alerts.find({}, {"_id": 0}).sort("timestamp", -1).limit(50)
    return await cursor.to_list(length=50)
# ── MQTT Bridge → MongoDB ──
def mqtt_on_message(client, userdata, msg):
    data = json.loads(msg.payload.decode())
    # Run async insert in background
    asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe(
        db.readings.insert_one(data), asyncio.get_event_loop()
    )
mqtt_client = mqtt.Client("fastapi_bridge")
mqtt_client.on_message = mqtt_on_message
mqtt_client.connect("localhost", 1883)
mqtt_client.subscribe("sensors/#", qos=1)
threading.Thread(target=mqtt_client.loop_forever, daemon=True).start()

# incident_reporter.py — AI-Generated Incident Reports
import anthropic, json, pymongo, datetime
from dotenv import load_dotenv
load_dotenv()
claude = anthropic.Anthropic()
mongo  = pymongo.MongoClient(os.getenv("MONGO_URI"))
db     = mongo["aiot_database"]
REPORT_PROMPT = """
You are a senior AIoT systems engineer writing an incident report.
Write a clear, professional report with these sections:
1. INCIDENT SUMMARY (2 sentences)
2. TIMELINE (bullet points with times)
3. ROOT CAUSE ANALYSIS (most likely physical cause)
4. IMPACT ASSESSMENT (what could have happened if undetected)
5. RECOMMENDED ACTIONS (3 specific steps)
6. PREVENTION (how to prevent this in future)
Use simple, clear language. No jargon. Total: under 400 words.
"""
def generate_incident_report(alert_id: str) -> dict:
    """Generate a full incident report for a given alert."""
    # Fetch alert data from MongoDB
    alert = db.alerts.find_one({"_id": alert_id})
    readings = list(db.readings.find(
        {"timestamp": {"$gt": alert["timestamp"] - datetime.timedelta(hours=1)}},
        {"_id": 0}).limit(100)
    )
    # Ask Claude to write the report
    response = claude.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
        max_tokens=800,
        system=REPORT_PROMPT,
        messages=[{
            "role": "user",
            "content": f"""
Alert: {json.dumps(alert, default=str)}
Sensor History: {json.dumps(readings, default=str)}
Generate the incident report.
            """
        }]
    )

    report = {
        "alert_id": str(alert_id),
        "generated_at": datetime.datetime.utcnow().isoformat(),
        "content": response.content[0].text
    }
    db.incident_reports.insert_one(report)
    return report

Solution: Distributed edge AI cameras with centralised alert management.
Component Technology Role
3x Raspberry Pi 4 nodes Distributed One Pi per camera zone
Pi Camera (per node) CSI Video stream input
YOLOv8n TFLite Each Pi Person and vehicle detection at 
edge
MQTT broker (central Pi) Mosquitto Collect all detection events
DeepSORT tracking Central Pi Track person across camera zones
SQLite (per node) Local Buffer events during outage
Flask REST API (central) Python Query events, retrieve images
React dashboard Browser Live map showing detections per 
zone

detection

 Note: 📌 This capstone project combines every skill from your 4-month schedule: edge AI (TFLite), IoT

n8n), and Linux systems (distributed Pi network). It is a full internship portfolio on its own.

glossary.definition: Artificial Intelligence of Things — integration of AI/ML with IoT devices for real-time local intelligence.
Running ML inference directly on embedded hardware (Raspberry Pi, ESP32, Jetson) without relying on the cloud.
TensorFlow Lite — compressed, optimized ML runtime specifically engineered for ARM processors and embedded microcontrollers.
Open Neural Network Exchange — hardware-agnostic open format for AI models, allowing easy conversion across frameworks (PyTorch -> ONNX -> TFLite).
Technique reducing model weight precision (FP32 -> INT8) for 4x smaller binary footprint and 2-3x faster inference speed.
Message Queuing Telemetry Transport — lightweight publish/subscribe network protocol designed for low-bandwidth, high-latency IoT devices.
Open Platform Communications Unified Architecture — standard industrial machine-to-machine communication protocol in Japanese smart factories.
Robot Operating System 2 — open-source robotics middleware providing nodes, topics, and services for autonomous systems.
Simultaneous Localisation and Mapping — foundational algorithm computing real-time position while mapping unknown environments.
Light Detection and Ranging — optical remote sensing technology capturing high-resolution 3D point cloud distance data.
Building software by articulating system specifications in natural language and directing AI code generation engines iteratively.
Large Language Model — deep neural network trained on vast text corpora (Claude, GPT, Gemini) capable of complex reasoning.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation — system architecture combining vector search retrieval with LLM generation for grounded, hallucination-free answers.
High-performance database optimized for cosine similarity indexing across high-dimensional dense embeddings (Chroma, Pinecone).
Python and TypeScript framework providing abstractions for LLM tool calling, memory buffers, and multi-step autonomous agents.
Extendable, open-source workflow automation platform running on Node.js with native support for MQTT, HTTP webhooks, and AI reasoning nodes.
Model Context Protocol — open standard designed by Anthropic for exposing tools, prompts, and database resources to AI models.
AI-first code editor built on VS Code with codebase indexing, multi-file edits, and inline agent capabilities.
The forward execution phase where a trained machine learning model evaluates live sensor inputs to generate predictions.
Elapsed duration from physical sensor signal arrival to processed output; mission-critical metric for industrial edge safety.
General Purpose Input/Output — digital pins on microcontrollers and single-board computers for reading sensors and pulsing actuators.
Inter-Integrated Circuit — two-wire (SDA/SCL) synchronous serial communication bus enabling multiple peripheral sensors per bus.
Serial Peripheral Interface — four-wire (MISO/MOSI/SCK/CS) high-speed serial bus ideal for high-throughput sensors and displays.
Core Japanese philosophy of continuous, incremental workflow improvements adopted across all top manufacturing facilities.
Essential Japanese workplace communication framework: Houkoku (Report), Renraku (Contact), and Soudan (Consult).
Japanese corporate consensus-building practice: consulting all stakeholders informally prior to official meetings.
Japanese-Language Proficiency Test — standardized evaluation scale ranging from N5 (beginner) to N1 (fluent native level).

commonMistakes.rule: Use 'a' before consonant sounds, 'an' before vowels, and 'the' for specific shared references.
commonMistakes.wrong: I built sensor system for factory.
commonMistakes.correct: I built a sensor system for a factory.

commonMistakes.rule: Use Present Simple for system capabilities (it runs), Past Simple for completed actions (I built), Present Perfect for achievements.
commonMistakes.wrong: I am built a classifier that is detecting anomalies.
commonMistakes.correct: I built a classifier that detects anomalies.

commonMistakes.rule: 'Know', 'understand', 'have', 'be' are stative verbs. Never say 'I am knowing'.
commonMistakes.wrong: I am knowing Python since 2 years.
commonMistakes.correct: I have been learning Python for 2 years.

commonMistakes.rule: Data is treated as singular/uncountable in technical writing. 'Each of the models is...', 'The team has decided...'
commonMistakes.wrong: The sensor data are showing high values.
commonMistakes.correct: The sensor data is showing high values.

commonMistakes.rule: Avoid literal translations like 'only', 'good name', 'do the needful', or 'revert back'.
commonMistakes.wrong: Please do the needful and revert back to me.
commonMistakes.correct: Please review the attached code and let me know your thoughts.

commonMistakes.rule: good AT (skills), experience IN (fields), experience WITH (tools), interested IN (topics), work ON (projects).
commonMistakes.wrong: I am good in Python and have experience on Raspberry Pi.
commonMistakes.correct: I am good at Python and have experience with Raspberry Pi.

dsaPatterns.title: Sliding Window Pattern
dsaPatterns.useWhen: Finding max/min/sum of a subarray of fixed or variable size. Problems: Maximum sum subarray of size K, Longest substring without repeating characters, Minimum window substring.

dsaPatterns.title: Two Pointer Pattern
dsaPatterns.useWhen: Sorted array, finding pairs that sum to target, removing duplicates, palindrome check.

dsaPatterns.title: Binary Search Pattern
dsaPatterns.useWhen: Sorted array, search space can be halved, or binary search on answer.

dsaPatterns.title: BFS Pattern — Level Order Traversal
dsaPatterns.useWhen: Shortest path in unweighted graph, level-by-level tree processing, minimum steps.

dsaPatterns.title: DFS Pattern — Graph and Tree
dsaPatterns.useWhen: Cycle detection, topological sort, connected components, path finding.

dsaPatterns.title: Dynamic Programming — 1D & 2D Templates
dsaPatterns.useWhen: Overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure (LCS, Knapsack, Edit Distance).

japaneseGrammar.example: センサーが動いています。
コードをテストしてから、デプロイします。
japaneseGrammar.translation: After testing the code, I will deploy it.

japaneseGrammar.example: エラーが出たら、ログを確認してください。
japaneseGrammar.translation: If an error appears, please check the log.

japaneseGrammar.example: データが多ければ多いほど、モデルの精度が上がります。
japaneseGrammar.translation: The more data there is, the higher the model accuracy.

japaneseGrammar.meaning: Can do ~ / To be able to ~
japaneseGrammar.example: ラズベリーパイで AI を実行することができます。
japaneseGrammar.translation: We can run AI on Raspberry Pi.

japaneseGrammar.meaning: Come to be able to / Start to
japaneseGrammar.example: 毎日コードを書いて、早く書けるようになりました。
japaneseGrammar.translation: By writing code every day, I became able to write it quickly.

japaneseGrammar.meaning: In order to / For the purpose of
japaneseGrammar.example: AIoT エンジニアになるために、毎日勉強しています。
japaneseGrammar.translation: I study every day in order to become an AIoT engineer.

japaneseGrammar.example: データを分析しながら、レポートを書きます。
japaneseGrammar.translation: I write the report while analysing the data.

japaneseGrammar.pattern: 〜てもいいですか (te mo ii desu ka)
japaneseGrammar.example: このコードを変更してもいいですか？
API キーを GitHub にアップロードしてはいけません。
japaneseGrammar.translation: You must not upload API keys to GitHub.

japaneseGrammar.example: バグを修正しなければなりません。
MQTT はこのプロジェクトに適していると思います。
japaneseGrammar.translation: I think MQTT is suitable for this project.

japaneseGrammar.example: センサーが壊れているかもしれません。
推論の速度は 50ms 以下のはずです。
japaneseGrammar.translation: The inference speed should be under 50ms.

japaneseGrammar.example: センサーが壊れそうです。
japaneseGrammar.translation: The sensor looks like it is about to break.

japaneseGrammar.example: センサーの種類によって、設定が違います。
japaneseGrammar.translation: The settings differ depending on the sensor type.

japaneseGrammar.example: MQTT プロトコルについて説明します。
japaneseGrammar.translation: I will explain about the MQTT protocol.

japaneseGrammar.pattern: 〜ていただけますか (te itadakemasu ka)
japaneseGrammar.example: コードをレビューしていただけますか？
japaneseGrammar.translation: Could you please review the code?

japaneseGrammar.example: ハードウェアだけでなく AI ソフトウェアも理解しています。
japaneseGrammar.translation: I understand not only hardware but also AI software.
